question:
Patient note:
A 52-year-old man with a decade-long history of chronic hepatitis C–related compensated cirrhosis monitored every six months by hepatology for small, non-bleeding portal hypertensive gastropathy walked into the emergency department at 19:25 carrying a plastic grocery bag lined with paper towels soaked in bright-red vomitus that he collected during his taxi ride from work; he explained that, over the preceding two hours, he had three bouts of forceful retching that filled a cereal bowl each time with crimson fluid and a few stringy clots but produced no dark, tarry stool or foul-smelling bowel movement, and his last defecation that morning had been light brown and well-formed. He denied passing sticky black stool, denied seeing coffee-ground debris, and denied ever losing consciousness or feeling the room spin, although he did admit to mild lightheadedness when standing quickly from a crouched position while stocking shelves at the liquor store where he is employed. He has never been treated for heart-pump weakness, sleeps flat without pillows, climbs two flights of stairs without shortness of breath, and has never been told his ejection fraction is low. Past medical records list esophageal varices banded two years earlier, splenomegaly with thrombocytopenia, and a remote episode of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis successfully managed as an outpatient; he abstains from alcohol since his antiviral therapy five years ago but continues to smoke half a pack of cigarettes daily. Medications include nadolol 40 mg nightly for portal pressure reduction, lactulose 15 mL with each meal though he admits poor adherence, and a multivitamin; he is not on aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants, steroids, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. There is no family history of bleeding disorders, coronary disease, or heart failure. Review of systems obtained in triage is negative for fever, chills, chest pain, palpitations, cough, jaundice beyond his baseline faint scleral icterus, pruritus, abdominal distention greater than usual, ankle swelling, bright-red rectal bleeding, hematuria, or weight loss. He arrived before any intravenous line, fluid bolus, vasoactive infusion, antiemetic, acid suppressive agent, or blood product had been administered and had been nil per os since lunch. Triage vitals measured manually with the arm supported at heart level recorded a blood pressure of 139/78 mm Hg, a regular pulse of 132 beats per minute confirmed on the bedside monitor, respirations 20 per minute, oral temperature 36.9 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. He appeared anxious but oriented, with cool clammy skin and a subtle teleangiectatic blush across the cheeks; conjunctivae were only mildly pale, sclerae displayed the chronic lemon tint noted in prior clinic notes, and oropharyngeal inspection showed fresh liquid blood pooling in the posterior pharynx without coffee-ground material. Neck veins were flat at 45°, carotid upstrokes brisk, radial and dorsalis pedis pulses bounding, and capillary refill two seconds. Cardiac examination revealed a rapid, regular S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, gallops, or displaced apex. Lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen was flat and soft; an old periumbilical hernia ring was reducible, the liver edge was barely palpable and nodular, the spleen tip descended to the left costal margin on deep inspiration, and shifting dullness consistent with trace ascites was present without tenderness, guarding, or rebound. No spider angiomata were visible on the chest, but two were noted over the shoulders; palmar erythema was present. Extremities showed no edema, and neurologic screening demonstrated full orientation, symmetric 5/5 strength, and normal finger-to-nose testing. Digital rectal examination produced a scant amount of normal-colored stool that did not stain the glove with black residue. A single 18-gauge catheter was inserted into the right antecubital vein solely for diagnostic blood sampling and type-and-screen; at that snapshot he had still received no crystalloids, vasoactive drugs, antiemetics, proton-pump inhibitors, or transfusion. Initial laboratory results available 15 minutes later revealed hemoglobin 15.7 g/dL, hematocrit 46 %, mean corpuscular volume 89 fL, platelet count 92 × 10⁹/L, international normalized ratio 1.5 (near his baseline), white blood cell count 7.4 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 73 mg/dL, serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.8), sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, albumin 2.9 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 66 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram performed simultaneously displayed sinus tachycardia at 131 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic changes. Upright portable chest radiograph showed clear lung fields and a normal cardiac silhouette; a single-view abdominal film revealed a nonspecific gas pattern without free air. The patient remains seated upright on the stretcher, connected to continuous cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring, awaiting urgent endoscopic intervention to identify and control the suspected variceal source of his brisk hematemesis.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses admission BUN, sex-specific hemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic disease, and heart failure. Before treatment:
- BUN 73 mg/dL (≥70): 6 points.
- Hemoglobin 15.7 g/dL in a man (≥13): 0 points.
- Systolic pressure 139 mm Hg (≥110): 0 points.
- Pulse 132/min (≥100): 1 point.
- Melena absent: 0 points. Hematemesis does not count as melena.
- Syncope absent: 0 points. He reported lightheadedness without loss of consciousness.
- Hepatic disease present (hepatitis C cirrhosis): 2 points.
- No history or clinical evidence of heart failure: 0 points.
Total = 6 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 9.
Final answer: 9
